national.title: Powerful Thanksgiving Day storm causes flooding, power outages
national.summary: The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of customers.
national.body: A Thanksgiving storm brought foul weather to the East Coast and Midwest on Thursday, causing major power outages, disrupting holiday travel and prompting the historic postponement of New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. More than 500,000 customers were without power Friday afternoon across the Midwest and Northeast, according to the utility tracking website PowerOutage.us. Of those, more than 122,000 customers were without electricity in Pennsylvania, along with more than 92,000 in New Jersey and 66,000 in Maryland. The outages reached more than 800,000 customers at the height of the storm Thursday night.There were 1,673 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday midday, with another 119 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. But that is a far cry from the more than 2,500 flights to or from U.S. destinations delayed on Thursday, while more than 460 were canceled, according to FlightAware.The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York, following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.Stormy weather creates havoc in New York CityNew York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning that two people had to be rescued from their cars because of flooding. He cautioned people not to attempt to walk, bike or drive through flooded areas. "We want to remind everyone to stay safe and there is no destination worth your safety," Mamdani said.The New York City Emergency Management agency reported that the city received 1.5 to 2 inches of rain on Thanksgiving, with some parts seeing up to 3 inches. High tides brought flooding to the city's coastal areas, including portions of Staten Island and Long Island.Central Park saw wind gusts higher than 30 mph, the agency said, while LaGuardia Airport recorded winds of 56 mph. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported. national.title: Pregnant inmate escapes in prison SUV after stop at Whataburger
national.summary: Rebecca Taylor, who was not restrained because of her pregnancy, slid into the front seat of the transport vehicle and drove away.
national.body: A pregnant prisoner is on the run in New Mexico after escaping in a corrections department SUV following a prenatal doctor appointment on Wednesday.Rebecca Taylor, 26, who was not restrained at the time because of her pregnancy, managed to slide into the front seat of the Dodge Journey transport vehicle and drive away as she was returning to Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants from the appointment in Albuquerque, according to the corrections department.Taylor escaped while the correctional officers accompanying her had stopped at a Whataburger, according to The Associated Press.The Dodge Journey was later located via GPS, but Taylor was no longer in the vehicle, corrections officials said. Her prison jumpsuit was found near the vehicle, the AP reported.Taylor is serving time after pleading guilty to four offenses related to the theft of a vehicle, vehicle burglary and receiving a stolen car, according to court records.She is from Cleveland, Texas, which is located outside of Houston, where she also has ties, according to authorities. Officials said they were following up on leads she may have taken public transportation and were checking Greyhound buses and Amtrak trains.The U.S. Marshals Service is offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to her arrest.Taylor is about 5-foot-7 and 180 pounds and has blue eyes and red hair. Authorities are asking anyone who sees her to call 911.All prison facilities in New Mexico were put on lockdown in the wake of the escape as a precaution. That lockdown was lifted at 6 a.m. on Friday.

national.title: Marching bands scramble to cover NYC costs after parade rearranged
national.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
national.body:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

national.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
national.summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
national.body:
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are now expected to improve, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.

More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.

One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

national.title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
national.summary: In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia.
national.body:
Manuel Valdes, Associated Press Manuel Valdes, Associated Press

KINGSTON, Wash. (AP) — Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her work day with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

Giles is tracking the Southern Resident killer whales, an endangered species whose population recovery is faltering despite years of protection. In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia. But in the last half-decade, the orcas have been hunting coho and chum salmon just north of Seattle during the fall.

It's providing an opportunity for collaboration between The SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. They're using drones mounted with petri dishes and microscope slides to collect droplets from whale spouts and employing a poop-sniffing dog to find stool samples, providing much-needed wellness checks for as many of the 76 remaining whales as they can find.

"They were here before us, long before us," said Giles. "They're a group of animals that are uniquely bonded to this place and to each other."

A research drone flown by Dr. James Sheppard of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance hovers over K33 "Tika," a Southern Resident killer whale, while attempting to collect breath samples, on Puget Sound near Possession Point State Park, Washington, on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by Lindsey Wasson/AP (NMFS/NOAA permit #26288-01)

Before colonization of the Pacific Northwest, the orca's main prey — Chinook salmon — weighed more than 100 pounds (45.36 kilograms) each and their numbers were abundant along the West Coast, Giles said.

But when American settlers came to the region, they built dams and overfished salmon. As cities and ports grew, boats created more noise, hindering the orca's hunting. Toxic chemicals flowed into sea water. And Chinook salmon now average about 12.5 pounds (5.66 kilograms), Giles said.

national.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
national.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
national.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

national.summary: President Claudia Sheinbaum blasted the DEA after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of interference.
national.body: Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson.Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs. "The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups.""It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added. Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?" Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism. "Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.U.S. steps up pressure on MexicoThe United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination."On Nov. 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "El Chapo Isidro," a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction. The secretary-general expressed solidarity with Kuwait and offered his condolences to the families of the victims, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. national.title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again
national.summary: The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
national.body:
BRUSSELS (AP) — After struggling to chaperone Europe's leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. "We didn't reach an agreement," he said.

Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.

The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.

Costa said "some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts."

It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.

In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.

In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.

Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.

national.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
national.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
national.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

national.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
national.summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
national.body:
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

national.summary: Caleb Williams put the Chicago Bears in first place. Joe Milton III put a dagger in his former team's season. Tyler Bass put the Buffalo Bills in position for a No. 1 seed.
national.body:
Caleb Williams put the Chicago Bears in first place. Joe Milton III put a dagger in his former team's season. Tyler Bass put the Buffalo Bills in position for a No. 1 seed.

The NFL's Thanksgiving Day tripleheader was filled with fantastic finishes that had a major impact on the standings.

WATCH: Stormy Thanksgiving weather causes delays and damages for many Americans

First, Williams rallied the Bears from a 14-point deficit and threw a perfect strike to Rome Odunze for a 6-yard touchdown pass with 3 seconds remaining to give Chicago a 39-35 victory over the Detroit Lions.

The Bears (9-2) moved ahead of the Lions (8-3) in a competitive NFC North that features four winning teams.

Then, Milton awed Fox analyst Tom Brady with a sensational performance, helping the Philadelphia Eagles beat the Dallas Cowboys 39-38 after overcoming a 21-point deficit late in the third quarter. Making his third career start with his third team in his third NFL season, Milton was 21 of 31 for 331 yards, three TDs, one interception, one TD run and a 121.8 passer rating.

After the defense sacked Dak Prescott on a fourth down, Milton completed two passes for 14 yards and Jake Elliott drilled a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds remaining. Milton was signed by Philadelphia off Dallas' practice squad last month after Jalen Hurts was placed on injured reserve.

The Eagles (4-7) have won two in a row to keep their slim playoff hopes alive in an NFC East led by the New York Giants (6-3-1). The Cowboys (5-7) saw their playoff chances take a huge hit, especially with a difficult schedule upcoming. Dallas' next three games are at Seattle (6-4), at the Los Angeles Rams (7-4) and home vs. Jacksonville (7-3).

national.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
national.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
national.body:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

national.title: Republicans rethink tariffs, giving Democrats an opening to challenge Trump
national.summary: After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda.
national.body:
Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press

Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hoping to blunt President Donald Trump's tariffs when they retake control of Congress may find partners in an unlikely place: among his fellow Republicans.

After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda. The administration proposed new tariffs on Wednesday targeting China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

WATCH: How Trump's newest tariffs could impact Americans and the economy

Whether Republicans actually buck Trump on tariffs could signal if election losses and the president's lame duck status shake what has been nearly lockstep fealty to him.

In interviews with more than a half dozen congressional Republicans since the election, most said they were open to reviewing tariffs, at least on a case-by-case basis. They expressed a desire for predictability and said Congress could reclaim its constitutional authority over tariffs. They were reluctant, however, to broadly curb the president's own tariff powers and acknowledged Trump could veto any repeal legislation.

But for Democrats eager to score some early bipartisan wins, the mere willingness of Republicans to revisit some tariffs could create an opening.

national.title: As Google threatens to cut schools' search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features
national.summary: The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA.
national.body:
Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

Jocelyn Gecker, Associated Press Jocelyn Gecker, Associated Press

Cheyanne Mumphrey, Associated Press Cheyanne Mumphrey, Associated Press

School districts are taking steps to block Google's artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America's classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.

The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board's A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America's classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google's suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.

national.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
national.summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
national.body:
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.

In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

national.body:
BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia's student movement on Friday announced the candidacy of chemistry professor Radomir Saicic for the upcoming early presidential election that will be held on Dec. 27.

The presidential vote comes after the student movement defeated former President Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, in an early parliamentary ballot on Oct. 25.

WATCH: Student-led movement ousts Serbia's right-wing ruler in historic election

Vucic resigned the presidency in September to pursue what turned out to be a failed bid to become the next prime minister after he and his party had ruled virtually unchallenged for 14 years. He served two near-complete five-year terms as president, and was banned by law from seeking a third.

Analysts predict the SNS would likely lose against the Students List candidate, and Vucic has suggested his party could boycott the presidential vote. It was not immediately clear what other candidates could join the race.

The presidency in Serbia is largely ceremonial. Under the constitution, the president commands the army and has a say in foreign policy but has no executive powers. While he was in office, however, Vucic concentrated power in the presidency, facing accusations of authoritarian rule. Vucic regularly announced important state decisions and policies and even presided over government sessions.

Saicic, who is 65, said, "It is time to restore dignity to the post of the president." He said Vucic had overstepped his authority while in office. Saicic promised he would "adhere to the mandate and publicly explain my decisions."

The youth-led movement won the election in October after leading two years of street protests that started in response to a train station canopy collapse in northern Serbia that killed 16 people. Many blamed the tragedy on alleged rampant corruption and negligence during the building renovation in Novi Sad.

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington, as new questions emerged about Europe's future financial commitments to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal.

The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin "my friend" at a recent summit in China as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."

"He can't be a friend," Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening the statement to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Zelenskyy's remarks. But Trump on Thursday defended his reference to Putin. "We want to make a deal. We want to stop the killing," he said.

"I could walk in and say, 'I don't like you!' and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin," he said. Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago, he added: "The biggest problem with that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

She isn't concerned about data that shows GLP-1 users eating less, she said."I see it as an opportunity to meet people where they're at, as they're continuing to evolve their eating," Barnes said. The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday. In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone. Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks, software providers and government agencies.Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said."In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

NEW YORK (AP) — Shoppers migrated from Thanksgiving meals to Black Friday deals as predictably as migrating geese heading south for winter, testing weather that had delayed the Macy's parade in New York and generated flood alerts in Southern California.

Black Friday, the U.S. retail industry's version of the Super Bowl, produces more foot traffic at physical stores than any other day despite growing competition from e-commerce and brands rolling out steep holiday discounts online weeks in advance, according to retail technology company Sensormatic Solutions.

Enough die-hard traditionalists still prefer hitting the shops as soon as they can after Thanksgiving that a line formed outside at Macy's Herald Square in Manhattan before sunrise.

Among them were Nita Lawrence and her two nieces, who were visiting from Miami and disappointed the department store's annual Thanksgiving Day parade was postponed until Saturday due to high wind warnings on Thursday. The three took consolation in exploring promotions that included handbags offered at 25% to 40% off and sneakers reduced by 20% to 50%.

"We do Black Friday every year, but this Macy's is much bigger. This is special," Lawrence said. "We're going to do some shopping and then we are going to the airport. Today, I am buying for me."

Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.

The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.

The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.

It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.

The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.

Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.

In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.

FILE - Actor Gerard Depardieu arrives to face trial for the alleged sexual assaults of two women on a film set in 2021, on March 24, 2025 in Paris. Aurelien Morissard/AP hide caption

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.

Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.

The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.

The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

national.title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
national.summary: The former Murdoch media executive was overheard at an event referring to the way Grace Tame was dressed.
national.body:
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.

Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.

In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.

Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.

She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.

"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."

national.title: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder
national.summary: The pregnant student was murdered after leaving a hotel with a journalist she had contacted to discuss her affair with the governor.
national.body:
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.

The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.

The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".

Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.

His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.

The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.

Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.

She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.

national.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
national.summary: The Ugandan army is helping the Congolese military fight an Islamist militant group in the east of the country.
national.body:
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.

The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.

The announcement comes days after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.

The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.

The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.

The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.

Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.

Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.

There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Uefa says it has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors "to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence" from the Marseille-Levski Sofia and Besiktas-Hapoel Be'er-Sheva games.

European football's governing body said it "strongly condemns the serious incidents of violence and disorder" at those ties.

It added: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.

"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety."

In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.

With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.

After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.

The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.

Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.

The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.

And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

national.title: Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
national.summary: Some parents, fed up with screens, have found an analog oasis in the role-playing game invented in the 1970s.
national.body:
First published in 1974, Dungeons & Dragons is now being embraced by a new generation looking for a screen-free hobby. Lauren Migaki/NPR hide caption

Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than 50 years.

In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10-minute piece on it in 1979.

More recently, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows including Stranger Things , a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns .

Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream — a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.

Culture Dungeons & Dragons turns 50 this year. Here's what the game has meant to you "It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of 9- to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."

Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens , a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host events like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.

local.title: Holley woman embraces her heritage and newfound sense of identity
local.summary: Bailey Kleckner discovered another part of her ancestry when she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan.
local.body:
If you had asked Bailey Kleckner five years ago who Two Clawing Turtles was, she wouldn’t have known — even though it was her all along.

“My given name is Two Clawing Turtles,” the 18-year-old said. “And that is to represent my two-spirit identity and also my fierceness as I have grown into my higher sense of being.”

Sitting at a picnic table at a park in Holley, Orleans County, Kleckner looks relaxed as she reflects on her journey.

“It was about five years ago now that I moved out here to Holley,” Kleckner said. “My story of even knowing my heritage really didn't start until I moved out here.”

Kleckner grew up in Chili, where she sensed there was something about her ancestry she didn't fully understand. It wasn't until her parents separated and she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan, that she began to discover that part of herself.

“Not knowing for so long, that was really life-changing,” Kleckner said of learning more about her Indigenous heritage. “It made me feel like I was finally at home.”

She later would go through the process to become an official member of the tribe.

The Onondaga Nation, one of the original five nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, bases membership on maternal lineage, according to Brad Powless, an Onondaga Nation council member.

Suzanne Schieres, lovingly known as Suzie, will be remembered for her strength, big heart, and unforgettable sense of humor. Famously funny, Suzie possessed a quick wit and sharp sense of humor that could instantly light up a room or put a smile on anyone's face.

Predeceased by parents, Edward and Geraldine Schieres and brothers, Nicholas, Michael, and Patrick. A beloved sister to Angela (Al) Valentin, Melissa (Edward) Mekus, Stephen (Karen) Schieres, a mother to Robert Glowniak and Kimberly (Jeffrey) Martin, grandmother to Taylesha, David and Julianna, great grandmother to Nalani and Bodi, and aunt of many. Suzie leaves behind a family and community who will forever cherish her love, laughter, and the memories they made together.

Suzie lived by a simple philosophy: "Have to have a good time in life because you can't take it with you." These words perfectly captured her spirit and the way she approached life. She believed in living every moment to the fullest, finding joy in the little things, laughing often, and making memories that would last a lifetime.

One of Suzie's greatest joys was Elvis Presley. She loved his music and especially adored singing along to her favorite song, "Love Me Tender." His music will forever remind her loved ones of her voice, her smile, and the joy she brought into their lives.

Though her passing leaves an immeasurable void, Suzie's legacy of love, resilience, and laughter will live on through the generations she leaves behind. Her family will carry her spirit forward in the stories they share, the memories they treasure, and the moments when they choose to embrace life just as she did.

Perhaps the best way to honor Suzie is to turn up the Elvis, sing along, laugh a little louder, love a little deeper, and remember her timeless advice to enjoy this beautiful, fleeting life.

Rest peacefully, forever in our hearts. May heaven be filled with Elvis music, and may you be singing along. You lived life to the fullest, and your love and laughter will never be forgotten.

local.title: Steelers are turning to Rudolph to salvage season
local.summary: PITTSBURGH — A season on the brink of crumbling. A disgruntled quarterback unhappy with the state of things. A team in need of a jolt. Mason Rudolph has been here before, and a lot of other places, too, during a nearly decade-long career that’s consistently thrust him into uncomfortable situations.
local.body:
PITTSBURGH -- A season on the brink of crumbling. A disgruntled quarterback unhappy with the state of things. A team in need of a jolt.

Mason Rudolph has been here before, and a lot of other places, too, during a nearly decade-long career that’s consistently thrust him into uncomfortable situations.

When Rudolph trots onto the field on Friday for the chaos-laden Pittsburgh Steelers (6-4) as they host Denver (8-2), he’ll be replacing a good friend and mentor in Aaron Rodgers, whose ugly departure this week shook one of the NFL’s proudest franchises to its very foundation.

And he’ll do it while playing for a head coach in Mike McCarthy whose reputation was forever tarnished and locker room presence diminished -- at least temporarily -- following Rodgers’ scorched-earth appearance on “The Pat McAfee Show” following the four-time MVP’s stunning benching and dismissal.

“Does it put some of us in an awkward space? Yes,” Rudolph said at the end of a dizzying 24 hours when he was thrust from trusted backup to starter. “But, again, it’s just another sort of opportunity to overcome adversity, and I think we’ll all look back on this as good experience.”

Or at least a defining one for both Rudolph and the current iteration of the Steelers.

If there’s anyone uniquely qualified for the challenge of picking up the pieces, it’s Rudolph. The checklist of things Rudolph has endured since being selected in the third round of the 2018 draft reads like something straight of Shakespeare.

There was the ugly brawl in Cleveland in 2019 that ended with then-Browns defensive tackle Myles Garrett ripping off Rudolph’s helmet and swinging it at him. There was his subsequent benching for undrafted rookie free agent Duck Hodges. There was the tie against Detroit in 2021 when he made a spot start after Ben Roethlisberger tested positive for COVID-19 less than 24 hours before kickoff. There was the promise that he was in the mix to be Roethlisberger’s successor in the spring of 2022, only to have the team sign Mitch Trubisky, then draft Kenny Pickett and bump Rudolph to the third string.

local.title: Sherman sets date for village dissolution vote
local.summary: Village of Sherman Board of Trustees, at their meeting this month, approved a resolution setting a date for a referendum on the possible dissolution of the village. local.body:
Village of Sherman Board of Trustees, at their meeting this month, approved a resolution setting a date for a referendum on the possible dissolution of the village.

The referendum, which uses the New York state mandated phrasing, reads: Shall the Village of Sherman, NY be dissolved? Village residents will vote yes or no to the question on Tuesday, Feb. 9 from 6 a.m. until 9 p.m. in the fire hall.

Prior to approving the resolution for the referendum, village trustees approved a resolution accepting and recording the valid citizen-initiated petition calling for the dissolution of the village. Village Clerk/Treasurer Jeanette Ramm confirmed that 145 out of 151 signatures on the petition were residents of the village and the village attorney found no deficiencies with the petition.

A certified letter confirming the validation was sent to Sue Oehlbeck who organized the citizen initiative petition, confirming the validation. “The process begins after our resolution tonight,” said Village Mayor Colleen Meeder.

The village will apply for a Citizens’ Re-Organization Empowerment Grant, administered by the state Department of State, which can provide up to 90% reimbursement funding for the process, up to a maximum of $25,000.

Trustees also authorized the village to retain a specialized municipal planning consultant to draft an objective pre-referendum study. This study includes an inventory of village assets, liabilities, structural service models and public informational reporting.

Meeder said that she and Ramm have already contacted the post office concerning a bulk mailing to all residents. However, a one-time bulk mailing would be more expensive than first class postage. Also, Meeder said, some residents have PO boxes, which are not accessible by the village. “There is no good way to do this. We’re trying to get out as much information as we can,” she said.

In a related matter, Meeder said the village is combatting the misinformation and the false narratives regarding the Sherman solar array. Rumors abound that the village is nearly bankrupt and that both companies involved in the solar array have filed for bankruptcy, she said.

local.body:
HANOVER -- The city of Dunkirk is not the only municipality set to lose its Community Bank branch in the coming months. The Town of Hanover was recently notified that the Silver Creek branch, located at Main Street and Central Avenue, is set to close in early 2027.

"Unfortunately, Community Bank is closing. We've received a letter," Lou Pelletter, Hanover Town Supervisor, said at a recent meeting. "We're going to be taking a look at what our future looks like with that."

Community Bank recently announced plans to close its Central Avenue branch in Dunkirk, consolidating its banking services at the Vineyard Drive location in the Town of Dunkirk effective Friday, March 19. Silver Creek and Hanover customers are now in the same boat as Dunkirk's customers. Community Bank said the decision was made following a thorough assessment of its branch network and how it can best serve customers as banking needs evolve.

Within eyesight of Community Bank is another recently closed business in the heart of Silver Creek, the former Rite Aid pharmacy. Pelletter recently met with Silver Creek Mayor Kathy Tampio, Deputy Mayor Jeff Hornburg, and a representative from the County of Chautauqua Industrial Development Agency (CCIDA) to discuss avenues for a new pharmacy to be located within the Town of Hanover.

At the recent meeting with the Village and the CCIDA, Pelletter provided all of the information he gathered from his efforts since Rite Aid closed. Pelletter previously spoke with Michael Pease, CEO of The Chautauqua Center, about expanding the center's Waterfront Pharmacy into the area. Pelletter remains optimistic about what could come next.

At its latest meeting, the Town Board approved new healthcare plans for eligible active employees and retirees. Active employees have a choice between Univera Bronze and Univera Gold plans, beginning Dec. 1. Retirees have the choice between Univera Senior Choice and Highmark of WNY Medicare Forever Blue, beginning Jan. 1, 2027. The Town covers 100% of the deductible costs for the Univera Bronze plan for active employees. The plans are in place of Independent Health, the Town's previous provider.

The Town Board also regretfully accepted the resignation of James Pinkowski as Hanover Court Attendant, effective Dec. 31.

In the month of October, the Town Clerk's Office collected $1,204 in State, County, and local revenue. The Clerk's Office issued 159 State Department of Environmental Conservation licenses, tags and permits; 41 dog licenses; three marriage licenses; and 11 handicap tags. The Code Enforcement Office issued 19 permits, of which 15 were in the Town and four were in the Village of Silver Creek, amounting to $1,200 in revenue for the Town.

local.body:
Early voting had already been underway for five days in late October when county and state Republicans gathered for a rally in Lakewood for what was to be a final push for the Nov. 3 election. One of the slogans used at the event matched those on signs scattered across lawns in Chautauqua County: "Fire Hochul."

Though this corner understands the sentiment and frustration, politics is unquestionably filled with retribution. In our staunchly red district, there are a cornucopia of reasons to be disappointed with how Gov. Kathy Hochul oversees the Empire State.

Her policies are often too far left for residents here who hold traditional beliefs. She is also pictured far too often with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, public enemy No. 1 when it comes to concerns about the nation moving toward socialism.

On the flip side, as a native Western New Yorker, she remains generous in supporting a number of economic causes in the region. Within the last year, the governor supported construction of a new north county hospital and played a role in expansion plans for Wells Enterprises in Dunkirk. Additionally, in June, she congratulated Jamestown for winning $10 million in Downtown Revitalization Initiative funding and Falconer for receiving another $4.5 million through NY Forward.

Despite these criticisms, one characteristic Hochul does not have is being delusional. Leave that to the chairman of the state Republican Party.

Within hours of overseeing another statewide shutout, Ed Cox demonstrated his obliviousness in a simple statement. "While Republicans fielded one of the best statewide tickets in living memory, we were not able to overcome the national political environment," he said. "Midterm elections are historically difficult for the party holding the presidency, especially in a second term."

Cox is a master at making excuses. His leadership -- as this corner has noted in the past -- is about as realistic as February camping in Western New York.

Republicans were not only thumped in traditionally blue New York, but they also were unseated across America in bastions that had been consistently loyal to the Grand Old Party. High gas and food prices, tied to an unpopular war with Iran, turned the tables nationally.

local.title: After big wins, pressure ramps up on Dems
local.summary: The final tallies are coming in, and the result is extraordinary. As of Sunday, Democrats have won the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades. Their Senate majority is the largest since 1992. They’ve even seized control of a majority of statehouses across the
local.body:
The final tallies are coming in, and the result is extraordinary. As of Sunday, Democrats have won the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades. Their Senate majority is the largest since 1992. They’ve even seized control of a majority of statehouses across the country.

All the more remarkable because they had to overcome gerrymandering by Republican-led state legislatures, ICE arrests, and Trump threats.

Hakeem Jeffries, who will be Speaker of the House, said on Sunday: “The people of our great country delivered House Democrats a historic majority with a mandate to fight for an Affordable America. Together, we will work hard to deliver the dramatic change in direction the American people are demanding.”

I don’t want to rain on Jeffries’ parade, but I don’t think this is what Democrats ought to be saying now.

Voters who have elected Democrats may think Democrats will be able to deliver “dramatic change,” but I don’t see how Dems can deliver dramatic change with Trump still in the White House holding a veto pen — and surrounded by belligerent fanatics like Stephen Miller, JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., and Todd Blanche. And when, behind them, the American oligarchy still has the reins of power.

Democrats have won by big margins, but not big enough to override Trump’s vetoes or the oligarchs’ preferences.

I’m concerned about the presidential election of 2028 when — after not getting anything done for two years and being blamed by Trump, Miller, Vance, et al. for everything that goes wrong in America — Democrats have to convince voters that they’re still the party of change that voters opted for in the 2026 midterms.

I speak from experience. The last time one party prevailed to this degree in a national election was in 1992. I was there, and I accompanied Clinton to Washington. The economy was shite. Expectations were sky-high for a sudden recovery, along with fundamental reform of healthcare, education, and much else.

local.title: Local health official recommends vaccinating infants against measles sooner
local.summary: The Monroe County health department wants children to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines as soon as 6 months old.
local.body:
The Monroe County health department is recommending that pediatricians start giving the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to infants as early as 6 months old.

The MMR vaccine requires two doses. The first shot is routinely given at 12 months and the second one between four and six years old.

Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown, Monroe County public health commissioner, issued the recommendation to vaccinate children earlier in response to the uptick in measles cases locally and abroad.

"We do have an increased risk of being exposed for our residents here, and that's why I have made this decision to make this recommendation for our local population," Vélez de Brown said during a news conference Tuesday.

She added that although no cases have originated in Monroe County, patients from nearby counties often seek medical attention in the area risking transmission within the community.

Vélez de Brown issued the recommendations right before the holiday season.

"Getting the early vaccine will help them (infants) develop their protection even earlier as we all gather in different parts of the country where there are numerous outbreaks occurring," Vélez de Brown said.

Patients who receive the early vaccine, she added, still need to take their routine shot at 12 months. For those who get their first dose at 12 months, officials recommend getting the second dose at least 28 days later instead of waiting four years.

local.body: The family behind the Blizzard of '77 Travel Game is bringing back this unique piece of Buffalo history to commemorate the upcoming 50th anniversary of those five fateful winter days.On the morning of January 28, 1977, just after 11 a.m., the blizzard began. Over the next few days, Buffalo and surrounding areas saw snow fall as high as 100 inches, with high winds creating drifts as high as 30 to 40 feet. The weather was so severe that President Jimmy Carter declared an "emergency" for the entire states of New York and Pennsylvania, the first time a snowstorm had prompted such a response.At the time, Buffalo resident Paul Marino was only nine years old."My dad, he was a salesman, and we were living in Buffalo, and he drove down to Jamestown the morning of the blizzard," Paul said. "He was coming back from his morning appointment. Around 11:10 a.m. is when the storm actually struck."According to Paul, his father, Chuck Marino, found the thruway route impassable. Attempting to turn around, Chuck found a handful of other motorists who had been stranded due to the worsening conditions. Eventually, he and the other travelers took refuge from the storm at a fire station in Irving for two days."During that time, we (Paul and his mother Donna) would check in with him; he'd give us a call, and he was explaining to us, Mom and I, what that experience was like trying to drive that." Paul continued, "My parents always loved playing games with me; they always encouraged creativity, so I took one of my dad's legal pads, and he hated when I did this, but I ripped off all of the paper so I could have the cardboard, right? entertainment.title: The Creator Of Peaky Blinders Is Also Responsible For This Influential Game Show
entertainment.summary: "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight is known for some hit TV shows and movies. Early in his career, he was also responsible for a major hit game show.
entertainment.body:
Knight — who has credits as a director, producer, and writer — is one of three people credited as the creators of the iconic game show. He shares the honor alongside David Briggs and Mike Whitehill, with whom he developed the show for the United Kingdom's ITV network.

The show's creation came early in his career, ahead of his significant feature film work, which would kick off in 2001. Because of this first major breakout project, Knight was able to work within the mainstream studio landscape, which helped pave the way for "Peaky Blinders" down the line.

"In the second ['Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?' program], there was a lady who opted to phone a friend and called her dad. But he didn't know the answer to the question," Knight told the Royal Television Society in October 2026. "The look on her face was like, 'Wow!'. And we realized this is actually drama." That drama was seemingly crucial for Knight's career, even if he didn't know it at first, as it allowed the powers that be to see how watchable his work was right from the beginning.

After unleashing "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" upon the United Kingdom in 1998 (and the United States a year later, as well as many other countries globally), Knight wrote some significant drama films — which makes sense considering his capacity for the dramatic.

His resume would go on to include David Cronenberg's mob tale "Eastern Promises" and Pablo Larraín's Princess Diana ghost story "Spencer." He is also credited as a writer on the new documentary "Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger," and is even writing the next James Bond movie.

entertainment.title: Percy Jackson EPs On [Spoiler]'s Surprise Return In Season 3: 'We Were Happy To Deliver That'
entertainment.summary: Percy Jackson Season 3, Episode 4 brings devastation to the gang - but also a welcome surprise! The show's EPs explain [Spoiler]'s big return to TVLine.
entertainment.body:
A lot goes down in Season 3, Episode 4 of "Percy Jackson and the Olympians," now streaming on Disney+ and Hulu. Some of it is excellent, like Kate McKinnon's appearance as Aphrodite, and some of it is terrible, like the untimely death of Bianca di Angelo . And somewhere in the middle of that spectrum comes the unexpected (and much-appreciated) return of Tyson!

Introduced in the Season 2 premiere , Percy's cyclops half-brother left to work at Poseidon's underwater forges in the finale, and many fans were convinced that we wouldn't see the character again until a potential fourth season. After all, Tyson is barely mentioned in Rick Riordan's "The Titan's Curse," upon which this season of "Percy Jackson" is based; in that third book, Tyson and Percy only briefly check in with one another through the use of god-powered video messaging, and their corrrespondence is relatively inconsequential.

So imagine our surprise when Tyson not only appears in Episode 4, but also plays a vital role in helping the group — four out of five, anyway — survive and escape the Junkyard of the Gods.

"The idea of having him in the season somewhere early-ish on was important, and that it was not an in-person thing, because he still should be working at the Cyclops forges," co-showrunner Dan Shotz explains to TVLine. "This turned out to be the perfect place for it, right? Because it's a Hephaestus domain talking to a Hephaestus domain, and Tyson's in a position where he can actually come in and really affect the story.

Adds co-showrunner Craig Silverstein, "I think it's what Percy needed in that moment , and it's what Tyson's character deserves after taking up such a huge part of our story in Season 2. It's much more satisfying to have him come in and, frankly, save the day than just sort of check in. We were super happy to deliver that."

Disney+ Actor Daniel Diemer tells TVLine that it was "so cool" getting a chance to return for "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" Season 3, adding that the writers "did a really great job ... at giving more of a glimpse into Tyson's world while everyone's kind of busy."

He also appreciated getting to drop by the set for his cameo because it meant spending more time with the other cast members, with whom he formed strong bonds while filming Season 2. When asked what he missed the most about his time away, he simply says, "the friendship."

Actually he says a lot more than that: "They're the best human beings ever," he says of his co-stars. "They work so hard, they're such a joy to be around, and they're so funny. I miss getting to hang out with them, so I'm really hoping we get a Season 4. Hopefully that puts me back in touch with them a lot more. But we've kept in touch, I've been texting them, and I was able to see a couple of them in between the seasons, which is great, but I miss seeing them every day."

entertainment.title: 5 Best '80s Sci-Fi Animated Series, Ranked
entertainment.summary: The '80s was one of the most important decades in the history of sci-fi animation - and these TV shows were among the very best of the decade.
entertainment.body:
CBS Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover There can be no question that the '80s was a peak era for sci-fi television, and particularly cartoons. Animation was the perfect medium for displaying on-screen technological advancements like CGI, and it allowed creators to merge influences from different genres and cultures, including cyberpunk, steampunk, and anime. '80s cartoons also led to a boom in tie-in toys and merch, and they introduced a lot of kids to mainstream comic book characters. Add to that the rise of consumer tech, like computers and video games, and you had a whole audience of TV watchers primed to embark on spacefaring adventures with their favorite heroes, or fight off the best cartoon villains right from their living rooms.

That said, it can be tough to navigate the universe of sci-fi animated shows from this era. Considering the sheer number of them, it can be even tougher to narrow them down to the best of the decade. Nevertheless, the mission awaits. Here's our pick of the five '80s animated sci-fi shows that we would send to defend the world.

Sandy Frank Entertainment In true sci-fi fashion, this first entry is two shows merged into one. "Battle of the Planets" and "G-Force: Guardians of Space" were English-dubbed versions of the 1972 Japanese anime series "Science Ninja Team Gatchaman." The premise follows a team of five teenage agents who utilize bird-themed uniforms and high-tech gear to defend the galaxy from evil. "Battle of the Planets" was the censored, more kid-friendly version of the story, featuring a lighter tone and less violence. It also introduced an R2-D2-like robot character named 7-Zark-7 and his dog, 1-Rover-1. "G-Force," the darker, more faithful adaptation, ran for 85 episodes, starting in 1986, before eventually becoming the first Japanese anime to land on Cartoon Network in the mid '90s.

This show was an interesting fusion of the power and limitations of '80s animated sci-fi. Viewers were introduced to a team who weren't related to each other, but who were competent, brave, distinct, and young. Their uniforms, vehicles, and abilities would serve as obvious influences for later shows — like the Japanese live-action series "Super Sentai" and the American "Power Rangers." However, the Western TV broadcast limitations that lingered from the '70s led to "Battle of the Planets" looking more like a "Star Wars" copy than anything else. Thankfully, "G-Force" offered a different tone for viewers. Later, in the mid-'90s, there would also be a three-part animated "Gatchaman" miniseries.

entertainment.title: In Praise of Andrew Scott
entertainment.summary: 'Elsinore' gives us the true story of Ian Charleson, an actor dedicated to playing Hamlet before his untimely death. The star turns it into a movie about a life
entertainment.body:
Elsinore is the type of movie that you’d assume was cooked up in a lab dedicated to concocting the perfect flavor of awards-season prestige-tainment. It’s based on a true story, involving extraordinary actor Ian Charleson, best know for his role in Chariots of Fire , given an even more extraordinary opportunity, i.e. portraying Hamlet at London’s National Theater in 1989. It’s a tragedy (Charleson was diagnosed with AIDS right before he began the play; he’d pass away several weeks after his final performance) that somehow manages to end triumphantly. It has moments designed to make viewers laugh, montages that rival any sports film’s training sequences, and entire sequences engineered to dehydrate audiences one crying jag at a time. It has the sort of symphonic score that leaves not a micro-ounce of doubt as to how you’re supposed to feel at any given moment. It’s a potent reminder that art is healing, our time here is short, and Olivia Colman in spiky, snarky mode should be categorized as a Class 1 narcotic.

But what separates this tribute to the need to thine own self be true from the usual glossy, touchy-feely melodramas that dominate the end of the year is the majestic presence, fretted with golden fire, at the center of it. The saga of one man literally dying to play one of the greatest stage roles ever written, not to mention the legacy of a thespian who left this mortal coil way too soon, rests on the extremely slim shoulders of Andrew Scott . The 50-year-old actor isn’t just up to the task. He is the supernova at the center of this film’s universe, the one behind the sound and the fury that signifies everything.

Scott has his own relationship with Shakespeare ‘s magnum opus, having played the melancholy Dane onstage in 2017. This would initially suggest an advantage in terms of playing Charleson, for whom taking over the National’s production (after Daniel Day-Lewis infamously walked offstage mid-performance) was too good to pass up. Until you realize, of course, that anyone who’d already inhabited that role for months on end would have their own interpretation embedded in their muscle memory and their bones, and suddenly the degree of difficulty seems staggering. Scott was not playing his Hamlet, but someone else’s. "Labyrinth" is a two-part historical drama based on the 2005 novel by Kate Mosse, which was a New York Times bestseller and won Best Read of the Year at the 2006 British Book Awards. Kirby leads the series alongside former "Downton Abbey" star Jessica Brown Findlay , with Tom Felton and John Hurt also in the cast and Ridley Scott serving as an executive producer.

The CW "Labyrinth" is set across two vastly different timelines. In 13th-century France, Alaïs (Jessica Brown Findlay) and her father protect a set of books revealing the Holy Grail's secret location amid the deadly Crusades. But archaeologist Alice Tanner (Vanessa Kirby) begins to have visions of Alaïs after discovering two skeletons and a labyrinth-engraved ring at an excavation site in modern-day France. Her discovery sends her down a similar path to Alaïs', potentially putting her life at risk. Sebastian Stan stars opposite Kirby in "Labyrinth" as Will Franklyn, an unlikely ally and romantic interest for Alice.

The 2012 series premiered shortly after Stan made his Marvel debut in "Captain America: The First Avenger" and over a decade before Kirby joined the MCU as Sue Storm in "The Fantastic Four: First Steps." Tom Brady called an NFL locker room a “very sacred place” as he weighed in on Aaron Rodgers’ abrupt Pittsburgh Steelers exit after the quarterback ripped into head coach Mike McCarthy .

While commentating on Thursday’s Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, Brady criticized Rodgers for publicly airing the Steelers’ dirty laundry.

“It’s a privilege to be in that locker room,” the former New England Patriots quarterback, 49, said during the broadcast. “You’re fighting with your teammates; you’re fighting with your coaches. You’re always acting as a team, together.”

“[It] shouldn’t always be the place for private things to become public,” he added. “That’s what I’ll say.”

Meanwhile, Brady’s co-host, Kevin Burkhardt, praised Rodgers, 42, as a “surefire Hall of Famer,” but admitted he was disappointed by the quarterback’s comments about McCarthy, calling it a “really sad way” for Rodgers’ career to come to a close.

Although Brady acknowledged Rodgers was a “tremendous” athlete, he stressed that his criticism had “nothing to do with his play style.”

“I was fortunate to be around a lot of great teammates over the years, and what made a great teammate, to me, was you cared about your teammates and your coaches, and you cared about what the team was trying to accomplish,” he added.

“That supersedes any individual aspect of your game that you want to promote.”
